paras: The Galloway robbery and lynching threat at Mount Pleasant was an episode in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, in October 1881, in which a crowd threatened to lynch two men arrested for robbing and beating a farmer, John Galloway, and assaulting his housekeeper. The threat, reported only by the Chicago Tribune, came to nothing: the suspects stayed under a deputy guard, one was later discharged and the other jailed at Greensburg.

On the night of Wednesday, October 19, five men came to the stone farmhouse of John Galloway, a wealthy bachelor of about 70 living about two miles from Mount Pleasant. According to the local report, they beat Galloway on his porch until he was badly injured, and one of them dragged his housekeeper, Nancy Newell, outside, bound her and "actually outraged her." The men took about $2,400 belonging to the two, discussed burning the house, and left their victims tied up.

Newell freed herself and went for help, swore out a warrant before W. N. Stauffer of Mount Pleasant, and described the attackers, while a reward was offered and a Pittsburgh detective was engaged. The Cincinnati Enquirer's Pittsburg dispatch, reprinted in the Chicago Tribune, predicted that anyone arrested nearby "would be lynched."

On October 21 two men were arrested and charged with the crime, whom the Tribune named as "Jack Newell" and "Chris Hodman," "well-known desperadoes" taken near Laurel Hill. The Tribune's Mount Pleasant item said they were held in the lockup under "a strong guard of deputies" while an excited crowd surrounded it and threats of lynching were "loudly made." No attempt on the lockup is reported in the coverage.

The Cambria Freeman reported that David Hoffman was discharged for want of evidence and Frank Newell was sent to the Greensburg jail to await developments, with the reward raised to $600. The same paper said a notions dealer, John R. Walker, had also been committed to Greensburg on suspicion and that further arrests were expected. No report of a trial or of Galloway's death was found.

Coverage centered on the robbery and the assault on Newell, which papers called an "infamous outrage" by "fiends" and "scoundrels." Only the Chicago Tribune carried the lynching threat, and it did so without comment, after printing a dispatch that treated lynching as the likely fate of any suspect. Pennsylvania papers such as the Lancaster Intelligencer instead described the arrested men as "sons of respectable farmers" and mentioned only "great excitement" in Mount Pleasant.
Midwestern weeklies reduced the story to a one-line brief that Galloway was "nearly murdered by five robbers," and no paper mentioned the race of anyone involved.

Accounts differ on the accused: the Tribune named "Jack Newell" and "Chris Hodman" and called them desperadoes, while the Lancaster Intelligencer and Cambria Freeman named Frank Newill or Newell and David Hoffman, young farmers of the neighborhood. The housekeeper also appears as "Nancy Norvill" in the first dispatch and as Galloway's niece in others.

reader.title: Galloway robbery and lynching threat at Mount Pleasant, Pennsylvania
bases: The only collective violence reported is a crowd surrounding the Mount Pleasant lockup and loudly threatening to lynch two arrested robbery suspects (A3); no attack on the lockup is reported, and no paper gives the race of anyone involved (A2, A3, A8).

No one was killed: the suspects stayed in the lockup under guard and were later jailed at Greensburg or discharged (A3, A8); the only mob action was a lynching threat by an 'excited crowd' of unstated size, reported by one paper (A3).

The robbery and the arrests are reported by several papers (A1, A2, A4, A8, A9), but the crowd's lynching threat appears only in the Chicago Tribune's Mount Pleasant item (A3), and the other arrest reports do not mention it (A2, A8).

framing.detail: Papers condemned the robbers as 'fiends' and 'scoundrels' and the Enquirer dispatch predicted any arrested man would 'likely' be lynched, without comment on the threat itself.
Midwestern weeklies ran only a one-line brief that Galloway was 'nearly murdered by five robbers'.
